content: Have you ever seen your parents buying wheat or rice from the market? Sometimes, there are tiny stones mixed in it. Or think about farmers harvesting fields. They get a huge pile of stalks with grain attached. How do they magically separate millions of tiny grains from the useless stalks and husks? Imagine picking them out one by one... it would take years!
If you have a mixture of heavy grains and very light dried leaves (husk), and you stand in a windy field, what would happen if you drop the mixture from a height? Would both fall straight down?

content.title: The Power of Wind
content.description: When the farmer drops the mixture, the heavier grains fall straight down forming a pile, while the lighter husk is blown away by the wind, forming a separate pile.

content: This method of separating heavier and lighter components of a mixture by wind or blowing air is called **Winnowing**. The word comes from the Old English 'windwian', which literally means 'to separate by wind'. Before winnowing, the stalks are beaten to free the grains, a process known as **Threshing**.

question: Which property makes winnowing an effective method for separating grain and husk?

content: Can you explain winnowing to your younger sibling? Why wouldn't winnowing work if both the components of a mixture have the same weight, like mixing sugar and salt?
Always remember that Winnowing is useful only when there is a significant weight difference between the two components. It's useless for separating two heavy things like stones and wheat grains!

Winnowing is deeply connected to ancient agricultural practices across India. It relies on a basic concept of Physics: Gravity pulls heavier objects down faster, while air resistance (wind) pushes lighter objects further away. You'll see this same principle used in modern air classifiers in factories!

Mini Challenge: Take a handful of peanuts with their papery red skin on. Rub them to loosen the skin. Now gently blow on the mixture while pouring it from one hand to another over a plate. Watch how the lighter skin flies away while the heavier peanuts drop straight down. You just did winnowing!

Imagine you accidentally drop a spoonful of precious salt into a glass of water. The salt disappears completely! Is it gone forever? If you were stranded on a deserted island with only salty ocean water, how would you get drinking water?
What happens to puddles of water on the road after it rains and the sun comes out? The water disappears, but where does it go? If that water had salt in it, would the salt fly away with the water?

content.title: The Disappearing Act
content.description: When heat is applied to salt water, the liquid water turns into an invisible gas (vapor) and rises. The heavy salt particles cannot turn into gas at this temperature, so they are left behind at the bottom of the container.

content: The process of conversion of water into its vapor is called **Evaporation**. It happens continuously wherever water is present. When this water vapor touches a cold surface, it turns back into liquid water. This reverse process is called **Condensation**.

Students often confuse Evaporation with Boiling. Evaporation can happen at any temperature (like a puddle drying up on a warm day), whereas boiling only happens at the boiling point (like water bubbling on a stove).

question: If you heat a mixture of salt and water until all the water disappears, what will you find left in the beaker?
options: A mixture of salt and water

content: Where else have you seen condensation in your house? Think about a cold bottle of water taken out of the fridge on a hot day. Why do water droplets form on the outside of the bottle?

These two processes are the engine of our planet! The Water Cycle (which you will learn more about later) is simply a giant, Earth-sized system of evaporation from the oceans and condensation in the clouds, bringing us fresh rain.

Project: Make a mini 'solar still'. Dissolve a spoon of salt in water in a small bowl. Place this small bowl inside a larger empty bowl. Cover the large bowl tightly with plastic wrap and place a small pebble in the center so the plastic dips slightly over the small bowl. Leave it in hot sunlight. Watch how pure water evaporates, condenses on the plastic, and drips into the large bowl, leaving salt behind!
